families.title: Lantern Wires
families.child_prompt: Tap a wire to change BOTH lanterns at its ends: bright becomes dark and dark becomes bright. Make the picture on the goal card.
rules: A board is a graph: lanterns are vertices and every drawn wire is a legal move.
Pressing a wire flips both endpoint states. It never moves a lantern.
The goal is the entire displayed ON/OFF pattern, including lamps required to stay OFF.
When a press budget is displayed, it is part of completion. Undo restores a press; every successful replay within the budget is accepted.
Every successful replay within the budget is accepted; the supplied replay is only a witness.
families.mathematics: Binary graph incidence: solve Ax = initial XOR target over F₂. A path changes only its endpoints; cycles change nothing. Every reachable target on a tree has a unique reduced edge set, while cycles create alternative solutions. Minimizing presses is the minimum-cardinality T-join problem for the mismatch vertices. This is a direct small case of combinatorial optimization, not a claim to teach its general algorithm.
families.prerequisites: Entry: distinguish bright/dark and follow a two-object change. Later: compare start and target, plan paths and cancellations, and count a budget up to six. Difficulty is relative within the family, not a grade ceiling.
families.natural_variation: Use a whole cycle, a complete binary tree, or every nearest-neighbor edge of a rectangular grid. Vary target patterns to expose endpoint cancellation, complements around a cycle, forced leaf decisions, and pairing choices.
families.guardrail: Do not make arbitrary switch subsets or special lamp exceptions. The graph comes from a named geometry; every edge uses the same rule. Do not call a target challenging just because it has more lamps. A budget should expose a specific alternative that fails, not conceal an unmotivated numerical restriction.
families.depth_assessment: Strong candidate. The entry pair is intentionally brief. Later wins require repairing a mismatch set, choosing a shorter cycle solution, or avoiding a locally attractive pairing. Rings alone have limited replay depth once their two complementary solutions are understood; trees and full grids are deliberate structural changes.

instances.title: Two neighbors
instances.prompt: On 4 lanterns in a ring, numbered clockwise: All lanterns start dark. Make only 1, 2 bright.
instances.hint: Find the wire that touches both goal lanterns.
instances.insight: One edge is one simultaneous two-state change.

instances.title: Across the ring

instances.hint: Try a path from 1 to 3; watch what happens to the lamp in the middle.
instances.insight: Two flips at the intermediate vertex cancel.

instances.prerequisites: Match two states; count to two.

instances.title: Repair the picture
instances.prompt: On 5 lanterns in a ring, numbered clockwise: Only 1, 2 start bright. Make only 2, 3, 4, 5 bright. Use at most 2 wire presses.
instances.hint: Which lamps differ between the starting picture and the goal?
instances.insight: The relevant target is the symmetric difference of start and goal; already-correct lamps need no net change.
instances.difficulty_step: The starting picture is nonempty. A child must reason about ON-to-OFF as well as OFF-to-ON; counting desired bright lamps is insufficient.
instances.prerequisites: Match two states; plan a replay of at most 2 moves.
instances.provenance: New initial/target pair built from the source binary-incidence model.

instances.title: Take the other way
instances.prompt: On 7 lanterns in a ring, numbered clockwise: All lanterns start dark. Make only 1, 3, 5, 7 bright. Use at most 3 wire presses.
instances.hint: The wire from 7 back to 1 is as real as every other wire.
instances.insight: The two reduced solutions on a cycle are complements. Pairing 1 with 3 and 5 with 7 takes four presses; pairing 7 with 1 and 3 with 5 takes three.
instances.difficulty_step: A tempting four-press solution fails the required budget; the win comes from changing the pairing around the ring, not from the extra two lamps.
instances.prerequisites: Match two states; plan a replay of at most 3 moves.
instances.provenance: New ring target and mandatory budget; source supplies the complementary-cycle method.

instances.title: Branches can cancel
instances.prompt: On a family tree: R above A/B, A above C/D, B above E/F: All lanterns start dark. Make only R, C, D, E bright. Use at most 4 wire presses.
instances.hint: Start at a bottom lantern: it has only one wire that could change it.
instances.insight: Leaf requirements force moves upward. The two C/D paths cancel at A; the R–A wire is not needed.
instances.difficulty_step: The topology changes from a loop with a global alternative to a tree with forced local choices. R must be lit without disturbing the already-balanced A branch.
instances.prerequisites: Match two states; plan a replay of at most 4 moves.
instances.provenance: New complete-binary-tree instance applying the source tree rule.

instances.title: A tempting pair
instances.prompt: On two straight rows A–B–C–D and E–F–G–H, with four vertical wires: All lanterns start dark. Make only A, B, C, H bright. Use at most 3 wire presses.
instances.hint: If you pair B with C first, how far apart are the two bright goals left over?
instances.insight: Pairing nearby targets greedily can be wrong: B–C leaves A/H four edges apart, totaling five. A–B leaves C/H two edges apart, totaling three. Full rectangular grids supply overlapping cycles naturally.
instances.difficulty_step: The board grows by one vertex from the tree, but the budget gets smaller. The difficulty is the pairing decision and temporary lamp cancellation.
instances.prerequisites: Match two states; plan a replay of at most 3 moves.
instances.provenance: New 2×4 grid target; no edges removed from the nearest-neighbor grid.

families.title: Clockwork Gates
families.child_prompt: Every bell makes the marker jump the same number of spaces clockwise. Set how many bells to ring so it first lands on the star. Later, one bell moves both clocks together.
rules: Positions are labeled 0 through n−1 clockwise; jumping k adds k and wraps around.
A jump counts landing positions, not positions passed over.
In count mode, choose a positive activation count before running the animation. The accepted answer is the first positive count at which every target is met together.
In gear mode, choose one fixed jump for the entire run; success is the specified first positive return time.
Reset and revised predictions are unlimited. No timing skill, written argument, or hidden feedback is needed.
families.mathematics: Translation in a finite cyclic group: x ↦ x+k mod n. One orbit has period n/gcd(n,k), but every shift is reversible whether or not that orbit visits the whole ring. The final linked-clock instances are an authored extension to simultaneous congruences in a product of cyclic groups; the shared activation counter is one orbit in that product.
families.prerequisites: Entry: follow clockwise landings and count to four. Later: coordinate two or three repeating sequences, starting phases, and counts up to twenty-two. Multiplication, gcd, and congruence notation are optional strategies.
families.natural_variation: Change ring size, a single uniform jump, starting phase, desired period, or couple two ordinary rings to the same bell. Select cases with a reason: wrapping, a proper orbit, two different generators of the same subgroup, or synchronization.
families.guardrail: Do not assign per-position jump exceptions, arbitrary missing landing sites, or a random menu of allowed jumps. Gear mode exposes the full stated integer interval. Synchronization changes the mathematical object to a product of two cycles; it does not add unrelated clues.
families.depth_assessment: Moderate candidate and a shorter content runway than Lantern Wires. Repeatedly tapping until arrival is shallow, so later completion requires a prediction of the first successful count, or a gear chosen for a specified orbit period. Keep the display concrete and allow replay. Once the child knows the orbit/CRT strategy, new numbers alone are practice, not new difficulty.

families.title: Mirror Couriers
families.child_prompt: The ball rolls straight from the bottom-left corner, bounces off each wall like light in a mirror and stops at the first corner it reaches. Shape the room or aim the ball to send it where it should go.
rules: The ball starts in the bottom-left corner and rolls in a straight line: one square right for every square up, unless the arrow shows a steeper start.
At a wall it bounces like light in a mirror. A side wall turns it back left or right; the top or bottom turns it back down or up. Each wall it hits is one bounce.
It stops at the first corner it reaches. Reaching the corner is not a bounce, and crossing its own path does nothing.
The path is drawn when you Launch, not while you change the room or the aim.
Can’t is a claim. After a launch it opens copies of the room, each copy corner marked with the room corner it folds onto; tap the corners that show no room works. A wrong claim gets one short answer.
In a find-every puzzle, Keep the rooms you think work and press That’s all; the whole shelf is judged at once.
families.mathematics: Unfold the room into mirror copies and the bouncing path becomes a straight line. From the bottom-left corner of a w × h room, going one square right per square up, the line first meets a copy corner q = h/g rooms across and p = w/g rooms up, where g = gcd(w, h). That corner folds onto the right wall exactly when q is odd and onto the top exactly when p is odd, and the ball has bounced p + q − 2 times. So a top-right stop takes an even number of bounces, a top-left or bottom-right stop an odd number, a single bounce means one side is twice the other, and the start corner is never reached: every copy of it is an even number of rooms across and up, and halfway there is a copy corner the ball reaches first. A steeper start (rise up for run across) only rescales: q = run·h/g′ and p = rise·w/g′ with g′ = gcd(run·h, rise·w). This is the unfolding used for billiards in rectangles and on the flat torus; the app makes no claim about irrational directions or ergodicity.
families.prerequisites: Entry: drag a corner, press Launch and watch where the ball stops; no reading needed beyond the goal line. Then count bounces, compare rooms that stop at the same corner, and read the copies of a room as a map. The corner-map claims ask a child to find every copy corner a given number of bounces away (across + up − 2), and the hardest rooms combine a steeper start with the room’s shape; these suit children comfortable with doubling and with odd and even, often grades 2–5 or beyond.
families.natural_variation: Vary the target corner and bounce count, the grid a room may fill, and the starting direction; aim by tapping a copy corner in the sheet of copies; ask for every room with a given bounce count; include one impossible target per set, answered with Can’t and a tapped certificate on the corner map.
families.guardrail: Rooms are whole rectangles with four mirror walls and the ball starts at the bottom-left corner. No obstacles, missing walls or one-off exceptions. The path appears only after Launch, so design is not a scan. Keep the first-corner stop exact and never confuse the room’s slope with the slope in the square grid.
families.depth_assessment: Shaping the room asks for the inverse of the rule; an impossible target asks for a reason, given by pointing at the copy corners a bounce count allows; find-every asks for a complete list and a reason it is complete; aiming in the sheet makes the unfolding itself the move. Once the reduced-ratio rule is known, new targets alone become routine; the steeper starts and the larger maps keep the hard set from being repetition.

instances.insight: Aiming at the copy corner a rooms across and b up (a and b with no common factor) stops the ball there after a + b − 2 bounces; it folds onto the right when a is odd and the bottom when b is even.
instances.difficulty_step: The aim replaces the rise and run menus: tap a crossing of the sheet, Launch, and the line folds into the path.
instances.prerequisites: Count rooms across and up on the sheet.
instances.provenance: Revision 1 asked for rise and run from menus in a 1 by 1 room (bottom right after 3); the card’s App fit replaces those menus by tapping a copy corner (4–5 Problems 3–4 sheet). Both old answers, 2 up for 3 across and 4 up for 1 across, are crossings here. The road’s 4–5 Mirror room.

instances.title: Aim in a wide room
instances.prompt: Aim so the ball stops at the top right corner after exactly 4 bounces.
instances.hint: The room is not a square, so the line to a crossing is not at 45°. Count rooms, not squares.
instances.insight: On the sheet only the rooms count: top right after four bounces is a copy corner 1 across and 5 up, or 5 across and 1 up, whatever the room’s shape.
instances.difficulty_step: A rectangular room: the aim in squares differs from the aim in rooms.
instances.prerequisites: Count rooms across and up; odd and even.
instances.provenance: Revision 1 asked for rise and run in a 3 by 2 room (top right after 4) from menus; now aimed by tapping a crossing (card App fit). Its answer, 10 up for 3 across, is the crossing 1 across and 5 up.

instances.title: A steeper ball
instances.prompt: Shape the room so the ball stops at the bottom right corner after exactly 9 bounces.
instances.hint: The ball now goes two squares up for every square across. Try a room wider than it is tall.
instances.insight: A steeper start rescales one side: with 2 up for 1 across, a w by h room acts like a 2w by h room at 45°.
instances.difficulty_step: A steeper launch: the 45° rule no longer applies directly.
instances.prerequisites: Count bounces up to ten; compare a room with its double.
instances.provenance: New in the app: no worksheet problem uses a steeper start. Revision 1 asked for a prediction in the 4 by 3 room with this start; that room is one answer here.

instances.title: Three bounces
instances.prompt: Shape the room so the ball stops at the bottom right corner after exactly 3 bounces.
instances.hint: Count the bounces of a few rooms that stop at the bottom right.
instances.insight: Bottom right after three bounces: rooms that in lowest terms are 4 by 1 or 2 by 3, and their doubles.
instances.difficulty_step: Two different room shapes give the same target; a doubled room does too.
instances.prerequisites: Count bounces; tell corners apart.
instances.provenance: Week 9 2–3 Problem 4 (design for a written target); target new. Revision 1 fixed the height at 6 and asked for the width; its answer, 4 by 6, answers here.

instances.title: Aim in a tall room
instances.prompt: Aim so the ball stops at the top right corner after exactly 6 bounces.
instances.hint: A top-right copy corner is an odd number of rooms across and an odd number up.
instances.insight: Top right after six bounces: copy corners 3 across and 5 up, or 5 across and 3 up.
instances.difficulty_step: More bounces, two answers on the sheet.
instances.prerequisites: Odd and even; count rooms on the sheet.
instances.provenance: Revision 1 asked for rise and run in a 2 by 3 room (top right after 6) from menus; now aimed by tapping a crossing (card App fit). Its answers are the crossings 3 across and 5 up, and 5 across and 3 up.

instances.title: Three up, two across
instances.prompt: Shape the room so the ball stops at the top left corner after exactly 5 bounces.
instances.hint: Try rooms twice as tall as they are wide, and count the bounces.
instances.insight: With 3 up for 2 across, a w by h room acts like a 3w by 2h room at 45°; top left after five bounces comes from 5 by 3 and from every room twice as tall as wide.
instances.difficulty_step: A steeper start and a bounce count: both the room’s shape and the direction matter.
instances.prerequisites: Count bounces; compare rooms with a common shape.
instances.provenance: New in the app. Revision 1 fixed the height at 8 and asked for the width with this start; its answer, 4 by 8, answers here.

instances.title: Eight bounces
instances.prompt: Aim so the ball stops at the top right corner after exactly 8 bounces.
instances.hint: Aim at a crossing and Launch. Does the ball always reach the crossing you aimed at?
instances.insight: The ball stops at the first copy corner on its line: aiming 5 across and 5 up stops it 1 across and 1 up. The answers are 3 across and 7 up, and 7 across and 3 up.
instances.difficulty_step: A copy corner that is not the first on its line is a trap.
instances.prerequisites: Odd and even; notice a line can pass an earlier crossing.
instances.provenance: Revision 1 asked for rise and run in a 4 by 3 room (top right after 8) from menus; now aimed by tapping a crossing (card App fit). Its answer 7 up for 4 across is the crossing 3 across and 7 up.

instances.title: Nine bounces
instances.prompt: Aim so the ball stops at the bottom right corner after exactly 9 bounces.
instances.hint: A bottom-right copy corner is an odd number of rooms across and an even number up.
instances.insight: Bottom right after nine bounces: copy corners across + up = 11 with across odd, such as 5 across and 6 up.
instances.difficulty_step: The largest sheet; several crossings fold onto the right corner with the wrong count.
instances.prerequisites: Odd and even; add across and up.
instances.provenance: Revision 1 asked for rise and run in a 3 by 4 room (bottom right after 9) from menus; now aimed by tapping a crossing (card App fit). Its answer, 8 up for 5 across, is the crossing 5 across and 6 up.

instances.title: The first crossing
instances.prompt: Tap the first point on the ball’s line where two walls cross.
instances.hint: Follow the line. It crosses many walls; find where it meets two at once.
instances.insight: The ball’s straight line through the copies stops where it first meets a corner of the copies: 3 rooms across and 2 up for the 2 by 3 room. The rooms it passed fold into the path.
instances.difficulty_step: The unfolding as a move: a crossing of one wall is not a corner.
instances.prerequisites: Follow a straight line on a grid.
instances.provenance: Week 9 4–5 Problem 3: the 2 by 3 table on a sheet of 4 by 3 copies; the line first meets a crossing 3 across and 2 up (facilitator answer). The fold replaces cutting and folding paper.

instances.title: A 4 by 3 sheet
instances.prompt: Tap the first point on the ball’s line where two walls cross.
instances.hint: Count the squares along the line until it reaches a corner of a copy.
instances.insight: For a 4 by 3 room the line first meets a corner 3 rooms across and 4 up: the ball stops at the bottom right after 5 bounces.
instances.difficulty_step: A wider room makes the first crossing farther away.
instances.prerequisites: Follow a straight line; count rooms.
instances.provenance: Week 9 4–5 Problem 4 (the 4 by 3 table: 3 across, 4 up, bottom right after 5), with the copy walls drawn; placing them is in the spec’s “Not yet done”.

instances.title: One bounce
instances.prompt: Find every room up to 6 by 6 where the ball bounces exactly once.
instances.hint: Start with rooms one square high. Which one bounces once?
instances.insight: The ball bounces once exactly when one side is twice the other: six rooms up to 6 by 6.
instances.difficulty_step: Find every: the list is judged as a whole, so its completeness is the puzzle.
instances.prerequisites: Count one bounce; doubling.
instances.provenance: Week 9 2–3 Problem 6 (every table up to 6 by 6 with one bounce; the facilitator lists six).

instances.title: Back to the start
instances.prompt: Shape the room so the ball stops back at the corner it started from.

solution.certificate: a copy of the start corner and a copy corner on the way to it

instances.hint: Launch a few rooms. Where does each one stop?
instances.insight: The ball never comes back to its start: every copy of the start corner is an even number of rooms across and up, and halfway there the line meets a copy corner where the ball stops first.
instances.difficulty_step: The first impossible goal; the claim points at one copy of the start and the corner the ball reaches before it.
instances.prerequisites: Tell corners apart; find a point halfway along a line.
instances.provenance: Week 9 K–1 Problem 6, 2–3 Problem 8 and 4–5 Problem 7 (the ball never stops where it started), answered with Can’t (card Decision: send it home).

instances.title: Three bounces to the top right
instances.prompt: Shape the room so the ball stops at the top right corner after exactly 3 bounces.
instances.hint: Launch rooms that stop at the top right and count their bounces.
instances.insight: A top-right stop takes an even number of bounces: its copy corner is odd across and odd up, so across + up − 2 is even. Three bounces is impossible.
instances.difficulty_step: The impossible target of the medium set; the claim points at every copy corner three bounces away.
instances.prerequisites: Count bounces; odd and even.
instances.provenance: Week 9 2–3 Problem 4, fourth target (top right after 3 bounces, impossible; facilitator answer).

instances.title: Eight bounces to the bottom right
instances.prompt: Shape the room so the ball stops at the bottom right corner after exactly 8 bounces.
instances.hint: Count the bounces of rooms that stop at the bottom right. Are they ever even?
instances.insight: A bottom-right copy corner is odd across and even up, so across + up − 2 is odd: no room stops there after 8 bounces.
instances.difficulty_step: The impossible target of the hard set, on the largest map; corners on the line that are not first on their own line may be tapped or left.
instances.prerequisites: Odd and even; add across and up.
instances.provenance: Week 9 4–5 Problem 6, fourth target, adapted: bottom right after 10 bounces became 8 so its map (9 by 9 copies) fits the board; both are impossible for the same reason.
